reason: The question asks for the most appropriate conveyancing route for three brothers who hold a single 30-perch Battaramulla land in undivided shares under a deed of gift that reserves their father's life interest. Deciding that route requires (i) the Roman-Dutch common law of usufruct, to say what the sons can and cannot do while their father's life interest subsists and what a deed of renunciation would achieve, (ii) the Roman-Dutch common law of co-ownership, to say whether a co-owner may sell an undivided share, build on the common land or claim for improvements, and (iii) the Partition Law No. 21 of 1977, for both an amicable deed of partition and a partition action. None of the three is in the corpus. The statutes that are in the corpus govern only the form of the instruments (notarial execution, registration) and the apartment Asanka wants to buy, which is downstream of the choice the question asks about.

legal_issues.issue: On the true construction of Deed of Gift No. 409, did Nimal gift to Asanka the entirety of Lot C (32 perches, with both buildings Nos. 400 and 400A), or only the building 'Waters Edge' No. 400A and the land on which it stands?
If Deed No. 409 exhausted Nimal's interest in Lot C, could Deed No. 429 of the same date pass any title in Lot C4 to Waruni, given that a donor cannot convey an interest he has already parted with?
Can the statutory registration priority in the Registration of Documents Ordinance decide the contest between Deed No. 409 and Deed No. 429, both being deeds of gift executed on 4th June 2001?
Does Waruni's claim, if it succeeds at all, extend to the buildings bearing Assessment Nos. 400 and 400A, or only to so much of them as stands within the 10 perches of Lot C4?

reason: Waruni's title to Lot C4 depends first on how much of Lot C passed to Asanka under Deed of Gift No. 409, and only then on whether Nimal had anything left to give by Deed No. 429. The first step is a pure question of construction of a deed whose recital is narrow (the building 'Waters Edge' No. 400A and the land whereon it stands), whose operative clause is ambiguous (a lot bearing Assessment No. 400A situated in Lot C, referred to the schedule) and whose schedule describes the whole 32-perch Lot C containing two buildings. The rules that resolve such a repugnancy - the primacy of the operative clause, falsa demonstratio non nocet, and the use of the schedule to identify the corpus of the grant - are Roman-Dutch common law and judicial authority, not statute, and none of them is in the corpus. The second step, that a donor cannot give what he no longer owns, is the common-law maxim nemo dat quod non habet, also not enacted in the corpus. The statutes in the corpus contribute only at the margins: they confirm that both deeds are registrable instruments affecting land, and they show that the statutory priority rule cannot decide the contest because neither donee took on valuable consideration. A complete answer therefore cannot rest on statute alone.
